facts.quote: The federal funds rate is the interest rate at which depository institutions lend balances at the Federal Reserve to other depository institutions overnight.
facts.claim: The fed funds rate is the overnight rate banks charge each other to lend the balances they keep at the Fed.

facts.quote: The FOMC holds eight regularly scheduled meetings per year.
facts.claim: The FOMC has eight scheduled meetings a year.

facts.quote: The FOMC holds eight regularly scheduled meetings during the year and other meetings as needed.
facts.claim: Eight scheduled FOMC meetings a year, plus extra meetings when needed (calendar page, last updated October 28, 2026).

facts.quote: so as to promote effectively the goals of maximum employment, stable prices, and moderate long-term interest rates.
facts.claim: The Federal Reserve Act gives the Fed the goals of maximum employment, stable prices and moderate long-term interest rates.

facts.quote: Even though the act lists three distinct goals of monetary policy, the Fed's mandate for monetary policy is commonly known as the dual mandate.
facts.claim: The Fed's goals are known as the dual mandate: maximum employment and stable prices.

facts.quote: low and stable inflation at the rate of 2 percent per year, as measured by the annual change in the price index for personal consumption expenditures, is most consistent with achievement of both parts of the dual mandate.
facts.claim: The FOMC's inflation goal is 2% a year, measured by the PCE price index.

facts.quote: Aiming for inflation that is a little above zero will, in normal times, result in modestly higher interest rates than would aiming for zero inflation.
facts.claim: Aiming a little above zero inflation keeps normal-time interest rates a bit higher than a zero goal would.

facts.quote: The higher level of interest rates in normal times gives the FOMC more room to cut interest rates to support the economy when it weakens.
facts.claim: Those higher normal-time rates leave the FOMC room to cut when the economy weakens.

facts.quote: The federal funds rate is the interest rate that banks pay to borrow reserve balances overnight.
facts.claim: Fed funds is the rate banks pay to borrow reserves overnight.

facts.claim: The FOMC's main tool is its target for the fed funds rate.

facts.claim: Short-term rates such as Treasury bill yields typically move closely with the fed funds rate.

walkthroughs.title: Who sets the rate
steps: The fed funds rate is what banks pay to borrow reserves from each other overnight.
The Fed's FOMC sets a target range for it at eight scheduled meetings a year.
The goal is the dual mandate: maximum employment and stable prices, with inflation at 2% a year.
T-bill yields track that rate closely. Long-term yields also price where it's expected to go.

walkthroughs.title: Reading the curve
steps: The yield curve lines up Treasury yields from the shortest maturity to the longest.
Normally it slopes up. January 3, 2022: the 2-year paid 0.78% and the 10-year 1.63%.
The 2s10s is the 10-year yield minus the 2-year. Below zero, the curve is inverted between those two points.
December 30, 2022: the 2-year paid 4.41% and the 10-year 3.88%. Inverted.

walkthroughs.title: 2022, the year of hikes
steps: The Fed's range started 2022 at 0% to 0.25% and ended at 4.25% to 4.5%, after seven hikes.
Markets didn't wait. Yields rose and stocks fell before the first hike in March.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq lost 33.1% on the year.
Growth stocks often lean on profits years out. A higher rate shrinks what those are worth today.

questions.q: Who sets the target range for the federal funds rate?
questions.why: The Fed's FOMC. It sets the target range for trading in the federal funds market. Changing that target is its main policy tool. Daily trading between banks then sets the effective rate, a volume-weighted median of real overnight trades. Neither Congress nor the Treasury sets the range.
questions.lesson_line: The FOMC sets the target range. Daily trading in fed funds sets the effective rate.

wrong.The US Treasury: Treasury doesn't set it. The FOMC establishes the target range for trading in the fed funds market.
wrong.The US Congress: The Federal Reserve Act sets the Fed's goals. Setting the target range is the FOMC's job.
wrong.Banks, by trading: Bank trading sets the effective rate each day. The target range it trades against is the FOMC's call.

questions.simple: The Fed's rate-setting group, the FOMC, sets the target range at its meetings.

questions.q: What is the federal funds rate?
questions.why: The overnight bank borrowing rate. Banks pay it to borrow reserve balances overnight. Other banks lend them from the balances they keep at the Fed. The FOMC's main tool is its target for this rate. It is not a long-term yield, a mortgage rate or the inflation goal.
questions.lesson_line: Fed funds is the overnight rate between banks. It's the rate the Fed targets.

wrong.The 10-year Treasury yield: That's a long-term market yield. The Fed targets the overnight rate, not the 10-year.
wrong.The 30-year mortgage rate: Mortgages are long-term loans. Their rates price where policy is expected to go, not just the overnight rate.
wrong.The Fed's yearly inflation goal: That's the goal for inflation, what policy aims at. Fed funds is a rate banks pay to borrow.

questions.simple: It's the rate banks pay each other to borrow money overnight, and it's the rate the Fed aims at.

questions.q: Fill in the blank.
questions.sentence: The Fed's dual mandate is maximum employment and stable ___.
questions.why: Prices. The Federal Reserve Act lists maximum employment, stable prices and moderate long-term interest rates. Even so, the mandate is commonly known as the dual mandate. Stable prices means low, steady inflation, not steady stock prices.
questions.lesson_line: Jobs and prices. When inflation runs hot, the Fed leans on rates.
questions.simple: Prices. The Fed's two goals are lots of jobs and steady prices, meaning low, steady inflation.

questions.q: The FOMC holds twelve regularly scheduled meetings a year.
questions.why: False. The FOMC holds eight regularly scheduled meetings a year, plus other meetings as needed. So not every month has a scheduled meeting, but an unscheduled one can still happen.
questions.lesson_line: Eight scheduled meetings a year, plus extra ones when needed. The dates are on the Fed's calendar page.
questions.simple: False, it has eight planned meetings a year, not twelve, and it can add extra ones.

reasons: the meeting schedule is a practice that can change (checked live 2026-11-12)

questions.q: The Fed's inflation goal is zero percent a year.
questions.why: False. The FOMC's goal is inflation of 2% a year, measured by the PCE price index. Aiming a little above zero keeps interest rates modestly higher in normal times. That gives the FOMC more room to cut rates when the economy weakens.
questions.lesson_line: The Fed wants 2% inflation, not zero. That buffer gives it room to cut in a downturn.
questions.simple: False, the Fed aims for 2% inflation a year, which keeps rates high enough to leave room to cut.

reasons: the inflation goal is a policy that can change (checked live 2026-11-12)

questions.q: What does the 2s10s measure?
questions.why: 10-year yield minus 2-year yield. FRED's 10-Year Minus 2-Year series is built exactly that way, and Fed researchers call it the 2s10s. It measures the slope between those two points, not the level of rates. Below zero, the curve is inverted between those two points.
questions.lesson_line: Long minus short. Positive is the normal slope, negative is inverted.

wrong.2-year yield minus 10-year yield: That flips the sign. The convention is long minus short, so an inversion reads negative.
wrong.Fed funds minus the 10-year yield: Some researchers pair the 10-year with fed funds, but that's a different spread. The 2s10s uses two Treasury yields.
wrong.Average of the 2- and 10-year yields: An average gives the level of rates. The 2s10s is the gap between them, the slope.

questions.simple: It's the 10-year yield minus the 2-year yield, the gap between long and short rates.

questions.q: An inverted yield curve means short-term Treasury yields sit above long-term ones.
questions.why: True. Treasury calls it inverted when longer maturities yield less than shorter ones. A normal curve slopes up, with longer maturities yielding more. Different spreads can invert at different times, so a curve can be inverted between some maturities and not others.
questions.lesson_line: Inverted: short pays more than long. It's the reverse of the usual slope.
questions.simple: True, inverted means short-term bonds pay more than long-term ones, the reverse of the usual shape.

questions.q: Fill in the blank.
questions.sentence: On Fed day, the FOMC statement comes out at ___ Eastern.
questions.why: 2:00 p.m. Eastern. One Fed statement reads 'For release at 2:00 p.m. EDT'. Another reads 'For release at 2:00 p.m. EST'. The decision is not out at the open or at the close.
questions.lesson_line: Scheduled FOMC statements come out at 2:00 p.m. Eastern, EST or EDT by season.
questions.simple: The Fed's statement comes out at 2:00 p.m. Eastern time on decision day.

reasons: release time is a practice that can change (checked live on the October 28, 2026 statement)

questions.q: The Fed raises its target range by 75 basis points. How many percentage points is that?
questions.why: 0.75. A basis point is 1/100 of a percentage point. So 75 basis points is 75 divided by 100, or 0.75 percentage points. It is a move in the rate itself, not a change of 75% in the rate.
questions.lesson_line: 100 basis points make one percentage point. A 25 basis point move is a quarter point.
questions.simple: It is 0.75 points, because 100 basis points make one percentage point.

deeper.example: The Fed's own table shows one: a 75 basis point hike took the target range from 1.50-1.75% to 2.25-2.50%. Each end rose 0.75 percentage points.

questions.q: January 3, 2022: the 2-year Treasury yields 0.78% and the 10-year 1.63%. What is the 2s10s, in percentage points?
questions.why: 0.85. The 2s10s is the 10-year yield minus the 2-year yield: 1.63 minus 0.78 is 0.85 percentage points. It is positive, so the curve sloped up between those two points, the normal shape.
questions.lesson_line: Always long minus short. A positive 2s10s is the normal, upward slope.
questions.simple: It's 0.85, the 10-year's 1.63 minus the 2-year's 0.78, so the curve sloped up.

questions.q: In a Fed hiking cycle, the 10-year yield tends to rise as much as the Fed's target rate.
questions.why: False. The Fed moves the short end. Long-term rates price where policy and the economy are expected to go, not just today's rate. In a tightening they tend to rise less than short rates. In 2022 the top of the Fed's range went from 0.25% to 4.5%, while the 10-year went from 1.63% to 3.88%.
questions.lesson_line: The Fed moves the short end. The long end moves on expectations.
questions.simple: False, long-term yields move on where rates are expected to go, so they tend to rise less than the Fed's rate.

questions.story: The curve starts with a normal upward slope. The Fed hikes at meeting after meeting. The 2-year yield climbs fast. The 10-year rises far less.
questions.q: What happens to the 2s10s?
choices: It inverts as soon as hikes start
questions.why: It shrinks, and the curve flattens. The 2s10s is the 10-year yield minus the 2-year yield, so when the 2-year rises more, the gap narrows. Fed tightening flattens the curve. It inverts only if the 2-year climbs past the 10-year.
questions.lesson_line: Fed hiking cycles flatten the curve, and sometimes invert it.

wrong.It widens; the curve steepens: Steepening means the 10-year gains on the 2-year. Here the 2-year is the one running.
wrong.Stays put; both yields rose: The 2s10s is a gap, not a level. When the 2-year rises more, the gap shrinks.
wrong.It inverts as soon as hikes start: Not at once. Tightening flattens the curve first. It inverts only if the 2-year yield climbs above the 10-year.

questions.simple: The gap shrinks, because the 2-year yield rises much faster than the 10-year yield.

deeper.trap: The answer depends on where the curve starts. From a normal, upward slope, a shrinking 2s10s means flattening. If the curve were already inverted, the same moves would push it further below zero.

questions.q: The Fed's range was 0-0.25% in January 2022 and 4.25-4.50% by December. How many percentage points did the top end rise?
questions.why: 4.25 percentage points. The top end went from 0.25% in January to 4.50% in December: 4.50 minus 0.25. It took seven hikes. The bottom end rose by the same amount, from 0 to 4.25%.
questions.lesson_line: In 2022 the Fed went from near zero to 4.25-4.5% in seven hikes, its highest in 15 years.
questions.simple: The top end rose 4.25 points, from 0.25% to 4.50%.

deeper.example: The Fed's table lists the seven hikes: 25, 50, 75, 75, 75, 75 and 50 basis points. They add up to the same 4.25 points.

questions.q: Rates jumped in 2022, and fast-growing companies still losing money got hit hard. What made them so exposed?
choices: Most of their profit is years away
Their sales drop as rates rise
questions.answer: Most of their profit is years away
questions.why: Most of their profit is years away. Higher rates shrink what future cash flows are worth today, so valuations can fall. Growth stocks that get more of their value from expected future earnings often feel that more. In 2022, investors stopped paying up for unprofitable growth and wanted cash generation.
questions.lesson_line: Distant profits get discounted harder when rates rise. That's a big part of why 2022 hit unprofitable growth so hard.

wrong.They pay the biggest dividends: Companies still losing money have little to pay out. The hit comes from discounting profits still years away.
wrong.Their sales drop as rates rise: Rate changes usually take at least a year to reach the wider economy. Stock prices react much sooner, through valuations.
wrong.The Fed targeted tech stocks: No. The Fed tightens to cool economic activity and keep inflation in check. Growth stocks feel it through valuations.

questions.simple: Their profits are far off, and higher rates make far-off profits worth less today.

deeper.counter: Higher rates don't automatically mean lower stock prices. Schwab says why rates rise, how fast, and earnings matter more. And 2022 also had sticky inflation and Russia's invasion of Ukraine weighing on stocks.

reasons: fixed before (q14 stem and why, 2026-11-09); sources differ on growth-stock sensitivity (see conflicts)

questions.q: Treasury yields rose and broad stock indexes fell before the Fed's first hike of 2022.
questions.why: True. The Fed's June report says the expected rate path started rising in the prior year's third quarter. Treasury and corporate yields rose with it, and broad stock indexes fell, before the first hike in March.
questions.lesson_line: Markets trade the expected path. By the time the Fed moves, much of it is priced.
questions.simple: True, markets moved months early, as yields rose and stocks fell before the first hike.

questions.story: Fed funds futures imply a 50 basis point cut. The Fed cuts 25 basis points. Stocks drop.
questions.q: Why can a rate cut push stocks lower?
choices: The bigger cut was already priced in
Any cut means the economy is failing
Lower rates make stocks less attractive
Stocks fall whenever the Fed acts
questions.answer: The bigger cut was already priced in
questions.why: The bigger cut was already priced in. Futures implied a 50 basis point cut, so prices already reflected it. A 25 basis point cut was less easing than expected, so stocks fell. Markets react to the surprise, not to the move itself.
questions.lesson_line: Markets trade the surprise, not the headline. What futures priced sets the bar.

wrong.Any cut means the economy is failing: A cut can come with a weak economy, but here the market wanted more. The miss versus 50 is the news.
wrong.Lower rates make stocks less attractive: The Fed says the opposite: lower rates can make stocks more attractive. The problem was the size.
wrong.Stocks fall whenever the Fed acts: No. Markets are unlikely to react to a move they already expected, and a surprise cut has tended to lift stocks.

questions.simple: Traders had already bet on a bigger cut, so the smaller cut let them down and stocks fell.

deeper.example: Flip it. Fed research looked at surprise 25 basis point cuts. On average, such a cut went with about a one percent rise in broad stock indexes. Same kind of cut, opposite reaction: what matters is the gap between what was priced and what came.

questions.q: What is the curve doing?
questions.why: The 2s10s is inverted, the 10y-3m isn't. The 10-year at 2.93% sits just under the 2-year at 2.97%, so the 2s10s is below zero. It is far above the 3-month at 1.90%, so the 10y-3m spread is positive. Different spreads can invert at different times.
questions.lesson_line: When you hear the curve inverted, ask which spread. The 2s10s often flips first.

wrong.Normal: long yields beat short: Not against the 2-year. The 10-year at 2.93% is below the 2-year at 2.97%.
wrong.Only the 10y-3m spread is inverted: It's the other way round. The 10-year beats the 3-month but trails the 2-year.
wrong.Both spreads are inverted: The 10-year at 2.93% still yields more than the 3-month at 1.90%. That spread is positive.

questions.simple: The 2s10s is inverted because the 10-year pays a bit less than the 2-year, but it still beats the 3-month.

deeper.trap: A headline that says the curve inverted may mean only the 2s10s. On this day the 10-year still paid more than the 3-month. The 2s10s tends to turn negative earlier and more often than the 10-year minus 3-month, so always ask which spread.

reasons: key rests on one Treasury row (f40)

questions.q: The New York Fed's recession-probability model is built on which spread?
questions.why: 10-year minus 3-month. The New York Fed's model uses the 10-year bond rate minus the 3-month bill rate. It turns that spread into the odds of a recession twelve months ahead. Market analysts more often watch the 10-year minus 2-year, and some researchers use the 10-year minus fed funds.
questions.lesson_line: Headlines watch the 2s10s. The New York Fed's model uses the 10-year minus the 3-month.

wrong.10-year minus 2-year: That's the market's favorite, not the model's input. It tends to invert earlier and more often.
wrong.30-year minus 10-year: That's the far end of the curve. The model pairs the 10-year with a short bill rate.
wrong.10-year minus fed funds: Some researchers favor that pair. The New York Fed's model uses the 3-month bill rate instead.

questions.simple: It uses the 10-year rate minus the 3-month bill rate to estimate the odds of a recession.

deeper.trap: The model gives odds, not a verdict. It turns the spread into a recession probability for twelve months ahead, using monthly averages.

reasons: key rests on one Tier 1 fact (f37)
the model's input could change (checked live: PDF updated 05-Nov-2026)

questions.q: 2022: the Fed hiked seven times. Which of these fell hardest on the year?
questions.why: The Nasdaq Composite. The tech-heavy index lost 33.1% in 2022, its steepest drop since 2008. The S&P 500 lost 19.4%, or 18.1% with dividends, and the Dow lost 8.8%. Energy stocks went the other way, up 59%.
questions.lesson_line: In 2022's rate-hike bear market, tech and growth took the worst of it.

wrong.The Dow industrials: The Dow held up best of the three, down 8.8%.
wrong.S&P 500 energy stocks: Energy went the other way, up 59% in 2022 as oil spiked above $120.
wrong.The S&P 500 index: It fell 19.4%, or 18.1% with dividends. Bad, but the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 33.1%.

questions.simple: The tech-heavy Nasdaq fell the most, down 33.1%, as rising rates hit tech and growth stocks.

deeper.trap: Check which measure a figure uses. AP gives the S&P 500's 2022 price change as 19.4%, but 18.1% with dividends. Compare price change with price change, never with a total return.

questions.story: The 2s10s dips below zero for one session, then bounces back. A friend says the recession is locked in.
questions.q: How much weight do you give that dip?
questions.why: Little. New York Fed research says inversions in daily or intraday data often prove to be false signals. Inversions that hold on monthly or quarterly averages are more reliable. Even a lasting one is a warning, not a recession start date.
questions.lesson_line: One day below zero often misleads. Inversions that hold on monthly averages are more reliable.

wrong.Full weight, any dip counts: New York Fed research found daily inversions often prove false. Inversions that hold on monthly or quarterly averages count more.
wrong.A recession began today: An inversion is a warning, not a start date. The New York Fed's model gives recession odds twelve months ahead.
wrong.Heavy, it means recession: Not for one session. Daily inversions often prove false, and Fed Board researchers say inversions are no standalone recession call.

questions.simple: Give it little weight, because a one-day dip below zero often turns out to be a false alarm.

deeper.trap: One session below zero is the kind of daily reading the research calls often false. Look for an inversion that holds on monthly or quarterly averages. Even then it is a warning, not a date.

questions.story: Over 2022 the 2-year Treasury yield rose from 0.78% to 4.41%. The 10-year rose from 1.63% to 3.88%.
questions.q: Where did the 2s10s end the year?
questions.why: -0.53, inverted. The 2s10s is the 10-year yield minus the 2-year yield: 3.88 minus 4.41 is -0.53. The 2-year rose far more than the 10-year over the year, so the 10-year ended below it.
questions.lesson_line: Short yields chased the Fed in 2022. That's what turned the curve upside down.

wrong.+0.53, normal slope: That's 2-year minus 10-year. The 2s10s is long minus short, so it's negative.
wrong.+0.85, unchanged: That's where it started the year, 1.63 minus 0.78. The ending yields give a different answer.
wrong.-1.38, far inverted: That's how far the spread fell over the year, from +0.85. The year-end level is what you read.

questions.simple: It ended at -0.53, because the 2-year yield rose past the 10-year yield.

questions.story: The Fed hikes 25 basis points, exactly as futures priced. Its statement signals more hikes ahead than the market expected.
questions.q: What's the real news for stocks?
choices: The higher expected path of rates
The hike makes stocks more attractive
questions.answer: The higher expected path of rates
questions.why: The higher expected path of rates. The 25 basis point hike was already priced, and markets are unlikely to react to moves they expected. The statement's signal of more hikes shifted expectations. Expected changes in the Fed's target move asset prices too.
questions.lesson_line: A priced-in hike is old news. The surprise can be the path of future rates.

wrong.The 25 basis point hike itself: It was fully priced. Fed research says markets are unlikely to react to moves they already expected.
wrong.Nothing, the hike was expected: The hike was, the path wasn't. A shift in the expected path moves prices on its own.
wrong.The hike makes stocks more attractive: Backwards. The Fed says lower rates can make stocks more attractive. A higher path of rates is the headwind here.

questions.simple: The hike was already expected, so the news was the Fed hinting at more hikes than traders thought.

deeper.trap: A headline like Fed hikes as expected can hide the real move. The statement's words about future rates can be the surprise. Higher expected rates shrink what future cash flows are worth today.

questions.q: After the 2s10s inverted in July 2022, a US recession followed within a year.
questions.why: False. The 2s10s inverted in early July 2022 and stayed inverted without a break. Reuters reported the run beat the 1978 record of 624 days, and no recession had come. NBER's latest business-cycle call is still the April 2020 trough. An inversion is a warning, not a timer.
questions.lesson_line: An inversion is a warning, not a timer. The 2022 one ran a record stretch with no recession.
questions.simple: False, the curve stayed inverted from July 2022 for a record run, and no recession came.

deeper.counter: This does not make inversions useless. Fed Board researchers say an inverted spread is not a standalone recession call: it largely reflects what markets already expect. Read the curve with other evidence, never as a countdown.

reasons: rests on NBER's dating, which can change (checked live 2026-11-12: latest call still July 19, 2021)

questions.q: From June 2022 into early 2023, broad stock indexes rose on net while the Fed was still hiking.
questions.why: True. The Fed's March 2023 report says broad stock indexes were volatile but rose moderately, on net, from June 2022. It points to easing inflation and resilient earnings. Meanwhile the Fed kept hiking, to 4.25-4.5% in December 2022. Rising rates don't automatically mean falling stocks.
questions.lesson_line: The market looks ahead. It can turn up before the Fed stops hiking.
questions.simple: True, stocks rose on net from June 2022 even while the Fed kept raising rates.

deeper.trap: On net matters. The Fed's report says indexes were volatile while they rose. A market can trend up through a hiking cycle and still swing hard along the way.

conflicts: Growth stocks and rising rates: Schwab (s25, October 2026) says 'Cyclical sectors and high-growth stocks have tended to be less sensitive to rising interest rates', while also explaining that long-duration growth stocks may face valuation pressure at higher discount rates (f64). Investopedia (s30) says the impact on valuations 'is often more pronounced for growth stocks that derive more of their value from expected future earnings' (f89), yet also that when the Fed raises rates 'toward the end of a boom cycle' technology and growth stocks 'often continue to do well'. In 2022 the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell hardest (AP, CNBC). The file teaches the discount-rate mechanism with 'often' and 'may', frames q14 on 2022 (barely profitable growth), never 'always', and q24 teaches that rising rates do not automatically mean falling stocks (f65, f29). Checker 2026-11-09: q14's why no longer says long-dated profits 'take the biggest hit' (no source says 'biggest'); it now rests on f64 + f89.

Which spread to watch: the Fed Board's FEDS Note (s22) argues the 2-10 spread 'offers a particularly muddled view' and that inversions are not independent recession measures; Investopedia (s31) calls the 10-year/2-year spread a relatively reliable recession indicator. The file never keys the 2s10s as reliable: it asks which spread the NY Fed model uses (Tier 1, s14), teaches that brief inversions mislead (s21 + s31), and uses the 2022-24 record (q23).

Investopedia's inverted-yield-curve page (s31) states the December 30, 2022 spread 'was 53 percentage points' and a 2026 spread '36 percentage points'; these should read basis points (Treasury's own rows give 3.88% minus 4.41% = -0.53 points). The file takes every yield from Treasury's rows (s15-s17) and cites no Investopedia number.

Effective fed funds rate: FRED's FEDFUNDS notes (s11) call it a 'weighted average'; the New York Fed, which publishes it, says 'volume-weighted median' (s13). The file uses only the New York Fed wording, and only in a wrong-choice note (q01).

The Fed's Open Market Operations table (s4) dates each change the day after the decision (March 17, 2022 versus the March 16 statement; its note corrects March 3, 2020 to March 4). The file takes dates from the statements and uses the table only for the count and size of the 2022 hikes.

Spread measures: Treasury's 3-month par-curve yield (q17) is a constant-maturity rate; the NY Fed model uses the secondary-market 3-month bill on a bond-equivalent basis (s21). The file reads Treasury's own numbers and never claims the NY Fed's monthly reading for a day.

Current policy, as of 2026-11-09: the Fed raised its range 25 basis points in September 2026 (to 3.75-4.00%, s4) and held it at 3-3/4 to 4 percent on October 28, 2026 (s8). Not quizzed: it changes every six weeks or so.

Track audit 2026-11-09: 2022 figures differ by measure across the track. AP (s27) gives price changes: S&P 500 -19.4% ('or 18.1%, including dividends', f69), energy stocks +59% and 'the only gain among the 11 sectors'. F7.09 uses the Select Sector prospectus's total returns: S&P 500 -18.11%, energy +64.56%, utilities +1.57%. With dividends utilities also rose, so q19's wrong note and f72's claim no longer say energy was the only sector up, and q19's S&P 500 note gives both AP figures. q24 and f29 now keep the Fed's 'on net': the S&P 500 made a lower close in October 2022 than in June (F7.04, F7.08).
